extracted.intended_audience: members of Congress, agency officials, administrative law practitioners, and lawyers drafting or applying the Administrative Procedure Act
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply the Committee on the Judiciary's explanatory standards for S.7 (the Administrative Procedure Act): requirements for public information, rulemaking, adjudication, hearings, examiners, limits on sanctions, and judicial review for federal administrative agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public information: required agency publication of organization and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency is required to publish in the Federal Register its (1) organization, (2) places of doing business with the public, (3) methods of rule making and adjudication including the rules of practice relating thereto, and (4) such substantive rules as it may frame for the guidance of the public. No person is in any manner to be required to resort to organization or procedure not so published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication must be kept up to date; required classes of informational rules must be separately stated (procedure distinct from substance, interpretation, or policy); internal delegations of authority must be published; the requirement forbids secrecy of rules binding the public and protects the public from being required to pursue unpublished remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication or availability of final opinions and orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required to publish or, pursuant to rule, make available to public inspection all final opinions or orders in the adjudication of cases except those held confidential for good cause and not cited as precedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must formulate and publish a rule respecting access to final opinions/orders so the public knows how to secure such information; authoritative 'rulings' or staff opinions, if authoritative, are covered by the substantive-rule publication requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to public records
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as statutes may require otherwise or information may be held confidential for good cause, matters of official record are to be made available to persons properly and directly concerned in accordance with rules to be issued by the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should classify data to specify what may be disclosed and how; rules must state how and where applications for information may be made, how determinations will be made, and who will decide; refusals of information are subject to administrative requirements (see section 6(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions controlling coverage (agency, rule, order, license, sanction, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions in section 2 are used to simplify later provisions: 'agency' excludes legislative/judicial/territorial authorities (with limited exceptions); 'rule' means any agency statement of general applicability designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law, policy, organization, procedure, or practice requirements; 'order' means the final disposition of any matter other than rule making (including licensing); 'license' and 'sanction' are exhaustively defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions determine whether a provision (e.g., rulemaking vs adjudication rules) applies; some agencies/functions (e.g., agencies composed of representatives of parties, certain war functions) are exempted from parts of the Act as defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking: general notice requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: General notice of proposed rule making must be published in the Federal Register and include (1) time, place, and nature of proceedings, (2) reference to authority under which held, and (3) terms, substance, or issues involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except where notice and hearing is required by some other statute, the notice requirement does not apply to rules other than substantive rules or where the agency, for good cause, finds (and incorporates the finding and reasons in the published rule) that notice and public procedure are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest. Agency notice must fairly apprise interested parties of the issues involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking: distinction among types of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act distinguishes substantive rules (subject to section 4 procedures) from interpretative rules, statements of policy, and rules of procedure; 'rule' is defined to include statements of general applicability but the Act treats categories differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some categories (interpretative, procedural, policy statements) may be exempt from full notice/hearing; agencies must still publish substantive guidance for the public (see section 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitions for rulemaking and agency response
rubrics_metrics.description: Interested persons may petition agencies to issue, amend, or repeal rules; agencies must consider such petitions and establish procedures governing petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee contemplated petitions as part of rulemaking procedure; the agency's action on petitions may be subject to the Act's public information and review provisions consistent with statutory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudication: different procedures and licensing treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill carefully distinguishes agency 'rule making' (legislative function) from 'adjudication' (judicial function). 'Order' and 'adjudication' cover final dispositions including licensing; where statutes require hearings for either rules or orders, the bill prescribes minimum hearing and decision requirements, but generally no agency hearings are required unless statute provides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing is specifically included as an 'order' but is exempted from some hearing/decision provisions (particularly initial licenses); the Act prescribes different procedures for rulemaking and adjudication and special treatment for licensing renewals versus initial licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of prosecuting and deciding functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Committee stressed distinguishing functions and separating investigative/prosecuting functions and personnel from deciding functions and personnel; where hearings are required, presiding officers (examiners) should be independent and not act as prosecutors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separation is central to preventing conflicts where the same persons both prosecute and decide; the Act provides structural protections (examiners' tenure, selection, and limits on delegation) to assure impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearings: presiding examiners and hearing powers (section 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where hearings are required by statute, one or more examiners appointed as provided in the Act shall preside at the taking of evidence unless the agency or one or more of its members presides; examiners may be withdrawn or removed if disqualified in a particular proceeding. Agencies may delegate enumerated powers to hearing officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision contemplates significant use of hearing officers; agencies may reorganize to appoint full-time hearing officers; charges of bias may be investigated by appropriate procedure and recorded in the proceeding's record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing evidence rules: burden of proof, cross-examination, and forms of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The proponent of a rule or order shall have the burden of proof (subject to statutory exceptions). Parties shall have the right to conduct such cross-examination as may be required for a full and true disclosure of the facts. Agencies may receive evidence in written form and are not bound by formal rules of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision does not preclude submitting technical written reports or field-survey material; whether the agency must produce the maker of a report depends on reasonableness; agencies may dispense with oral evidence only in enumerated proceedings where seeing/hearing witnesses is not necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive record for decision and official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The transcript of testimony and exhibits, together with all papers and requests filed in the proceeding, shall constitute the exclusive record for decision in cases covered by section 7; the agency may take official notice of material facts not appearing in the record if stated in the record or decision, but any party affected shall on timely request be afforded an opportunity to show the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 7 and 8 apply where decisions are to be based on the hearing record; certain classes of cases (inspections, tests, elections) are excluded; the official-notice mechanism permits reliance on extra-record facts only with chance for rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisions: initial decisions, recommended decisions, and agency review (section 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the agency or a subordinate hearing officer may make the initial decision; where the agency did not preside, a recommended decision by the officer who presided shall be filed (with limited exceptions for rulemaking and initial licenses); parties shall have a timely opportunity to submit proposed findings and conclusions and to file exceptions upon agency review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon review the agency may limit review to legal questions or whether findings are supported by substantial evidence, may take new evidence, remand, or make new findings; exceptions permit parties to present contentions before final decision; certain expedited exceptions exist for tentative decisions or when due and timely execution imperatively requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to submit proposed findings and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to each recommended, initial, or tentative decision, parties shall have a timely opportunity to submit proposed findings and conclusions, and prior to each decision upon agency review, to submit exceptions to the initial, recommended, or tentative decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject to agency rules, proposed findings or exceptions may be oral where adequate; this ensures parties can present their legal and factual objections before the agency issues a final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation to hearing officers
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency may delegate to a hearing officer any of the enumerated powers with which it is vested; the enumeration of hearing-officer powers is not intended to be exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegations must be consistent with the Act's separation-of-functions principles and with published rules of organization and procedure; agencies may delegate many procedural powers to presiding officers but must respect other Act requirements (e.g., recommended decisions when agency does not preside).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners: appointment, civil-service selection, compensation, and tenure (section 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointments of examiners are to be made by employing agencies of personnel determined by the Civil Service Commission to be qualified and competent; examiners shall serve 'only as examiners' except in limited instances; they are subject to removal only for good cause 'established and determined' by the Commission, which must afford a hearing if requested and base its decision solely on the record of that hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Civil Service Commission prescribes compensation in accordance with classification schedules (though the efficiency rating system does not apply to examiners); agencies should use examiners in rotation where practicable; examiners' removal protections are intended to assure independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on sanctions and treatment of licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 9 limits administrative sanctions and prescribes rules relating to licenses — grants, revocations, renewals — distinguishing initial licenses from renewals and providing for codification of best existing law and practice on sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsection (b) codifies best existing law related to sanctions and is not intended to preclude temporary licenses pending application determinations; sanctions are broadly defined (e.g., prohibitions, penalties, seizures, assessments, requirements, restrictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review: entitlement and limits (section 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person suffering legal wrong because of any agency action, or adversely affected or aggrieved by such action within the meaning of any relevant statute, shall be entitled to judicial review of such action, except insofar as statutes preclude it or agency action is by law committed to agency discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a specific statutory judicial-review method exists it shall be used; otherwise any applicable judicial procedure (injunction, declaratory judgment, habeas corpus) is available; reviewable acts include rules, orders, licenses, sanctions, relief, denials, and failures to act as defined in the Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review: exhaustion, form, venue, and interim relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of exhaustion of administrative remedies is intended to apply only where expressly required by statute or where agency rules require subordinate decisions be appealed before finality for review purposes; interim relief (e.g., staying enforcement) may be granted where necessary to prevent irreparable injury consistent with court powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a specific statutory review procedure is inadequate, courts may grant other remedies; the Act preserves existing enforcement procedures; interim relief availability may differ from past interpretations but remains subject to irreparable-injury and other equitable considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of judicial review: substantial evidence and prejudicial error
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of review declares existing law: courts review findings for 'substantial evidence' (such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion); the Act adopts the common-law rule that error is not fatal unless prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review includes consideration whether orders have a rational probative basis; courts retain power to compel agency action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed but are not to assume nonjudicial functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from notice/hearing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 exempts from notice/hearing requirements rulemaking involving (1) military, naval, or foreign affairs functions, or (2) matters relating to agency management or personnel or to public property, loans, grants, benefits, or contracts; exemptions apply 'to the extent' the subject is directly involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions do not relieve agencies from requirements imposed by other statutes; 'foreign affairs functions' should be narrowly interpreted; exceptions permit agencies discretion to adopt voluntary public rulemaking procedures where useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause exception to notice for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may find and incorporate in the published rule that notice and public procedure are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest, thereby dispensing with the notice requirement for that rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such findings must be incorporated and reasoned in the published rule; the good-cause finding is the narrow exception to the general notice-and-comment obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to conduct cross-examination and to representation at hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties shall have the right to conduct cross-examination as required for full disclosure of facts, and procedures presume parties may appear and present their case (including counsel and oral or written submissions subject to agency rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject to the agency's rules, proposed findings or exceptions may be oral where adequate; agencies may limit oral evidence in certain enumerated proceedings but generally must permit effective opportunity to present and challenge evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency cannot require resort to unpublished procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: No person is to be required to resort to organization or procedure not published by the agency; the subsection forbids secrecy of rules binding or applicable to the public or of delegations of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects the public from being forced to follow non-public internal procedures and ensures transparency of administrative process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors in procedure not automatically fatal — prejudicial error rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute adopts the rule that not every failure to observe requirements of the statute is ipso facto fatal to the validity of an order; error is not fatal unless prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should focus on whether procedural errors harmed the party's rights or the integrity of the decision rather than invalidate orders for harmless mistakes.
